performers: Dietrich Fischer-Dieskau, baritone; Berlin Philharmonic; Rudolf Kempe, conductor
intro: A mother comes through the door; the father looks down for the little face beside her. Dietrich Fischer-Dieskau sings this scene with Rudolf Kempe and the Berlin Philharmonic, in a song whose orchestra has no violins.

sections.label: A · The empty place by the door
sections.mNote: Cor anglais and bassoons above plucked cellos

sections.label: A′ · The mother brings a candle
sections.mNote: Harp and plucked double bass renew the opening

sections.label: Coda · Cor anglais after the lament
sections.mNote: Horns and bowed cellos; a G-major ending

cues.title: An orchestra without violins
cues.text: Cor anglais and bassoons wind around one another above plucked cellos. Mahler marks the opening “Schwer, dumpf” — heavy, muffled. Fischer-Dieskau joins an orchestra stripped of violins for the whole song.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Kindertotenlieder, C. F. Kahnt full score, plate 4460 (1905), p. 33: instrumentation and opening marking; our translation. https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=18417&itemFileId=62425
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: At the child’s height
cues.text: Rückert’s father turns towards his wife, then looks below her face: “näher nach der Schwelle” — nearer the threshold. His eyes still expect the daughter who used to come in beside her. The room remembers a habit the father cannot stop.
cues.evidence: Rückert, Wenn dein Mütterlein, first stanza as set by Mahler; German text at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kindertotenlieder#Text. Our translation.

cues.title: A nursery tune for a lost child
cues.text: The voice sings in the shape of a nursery song, even of a chanted counting rhyme, and tries in vain to bring the child back. Beneath it the orchestra moves at twice the voice’s speed, in lines that recall the first song.
cues.evidence: Reinhold Kubik, Universal Edition introduction to Kindertotenlieder (autumn 2008), on song 3: children’s-song melodies, counting rhymes, and a linear accompaniment moving twice as fast as the voice and recalling the first song: https://www.universaledition.com/en/Kindertotenlieder/P0045027

cues.title: The doorway again
cues.text: The cor anglais begins again, now with harp and plucked double bass underneath. In the second stanza the mother carries a candle, and the child seems to slip into the room behind her. Fischer-Dieskau’s closing lament calls her a light extinguished too soon.
cues.evidence: Kahnt full score, pp. 40–46, rehearsal 3 onwards; Rückert’s second stanza. The changed bass scoring is discussed at https://geertwoltjer.nl/Songs/MahlerAnalysis/Mahler3.html
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A chamber orchestra in a small hall
cues.text: Mahler prefers small rooms for these songs: the Kleiner Musikvereinssaal for the Vienna performances of 1905, then the Stephaniesaal in Graz. His string section has about ten first violins at most. This song has no violins at all.
cues.evidence: Mahler catalogue, Kindertotenlieder, scoring note: good evidence that the small venues were the composer’s own choice and that the strings were probably no more than 10, 8, 6, 6 and 4 (citing Hefling and Hilmar-Voit). Performances: Vienna 29 January and 3 February 1905, Graz 1 June 1905: https://www.mahlercat.org.uk/Pages/KtL/KtL.htm

cues.title: “Don’t tempt Providence”
cues.text: Alma Mahler cannot understand how her husband can bewail the deaths of children “in the best of health and spirits” within an hour of kissing his own. She exclaims: “For Heaven’s sake, don’t tempt Providence!” Mahler completes the cycle in the summer of 1904.
cues.evidence: Alma Mahler, Gustav Mahler: Memories and Letters, as quoted by Georg Predota, Interlude, 29 January 2019: https://interlude.hk/mahler-kindertotenlieder-premiered-today-1905/. The exclamation is also given in Michael Kennedy, Mahler (Master Musicians), Edward Seckerson, Mahler: His Life and Times (1982), and Stephen Johnson, Mahler (2007) (full-text excerpts seen); the memoir itself was not opened. Kubik dates songs 2 and 5 to 1904: https://www.universaledition.com/en/Kindertotenlieder/P0045027

cues.title: The cellos take their bows
cues.text: The cor anglais recalls the opening after the voice has finished. The cellos now bow their notes, with horns close beside them. The song comes to rest on G major, the chord that would normally lead back to C minor.
cues.evidence: Kahnt full score, p. 47: Wieder wie zu Anfang, bowed cellos, horns and the final dominant chord. https://geertwoltjer.nl/Songs/MahlerAnalysis/Mahler3.html
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: A new bass beneath the doorway
transitions.from: A · The empty place by the door
transitions.to: A′ · The mother brings a candle
transitions.how: The first stanza descends to its low “Töchterlein” and closes in C minor. After the ritardando, Wie zu Anfang restores the opening pace and cor anglais tune. Harp and plucked double bass replace the cello pulse; a held bass-clarinet note crosses the join.
transitions.evidence: Kahnt full score, p. 40, rehearsal 3; Woltjer, song III, bars 31–33. https://geertwoltjer.nl/Songs/MahlerAnalysis/Mahler3.html

transitions.title: Bowed cellos replace the plucked pulse
transitions.from: A′ · The mother brings a candle
transitions.to: Coda · Cor anglais after the lament
transitions.how: Wieder wie zu Anfang brings the cor anglais back, with horns and bowed cellos beneath it. The wind phrases lengthen and slow. Harp and low strings support a final G-major chord, C minor’s dominant, held under fermatas.
transitions.evidence: Kahnt full score, p. 47. The dominant ending is discussed at https://geertwoltjer.nl/Songs/MahlerAnalysis/Mahler3.html

source.title: Mahler, Kindertotenlieder, full score (C. F. Kahnt, plate 4460)
source.locator: Song III, printed pp. 33–47: cor anglais and plucked cellos at the opening, harp and double basses in the second stanza. Violins are silent throughout.

timeline.note: Opening: cor anglais and bassoon lines above the pizzicato cello pulse.
The baritone joins the cor anglais and bassoons above plucked cellos.
Harp and plucked double basses replace the cellos beneath the returning cor anglais phrase.
Cor anglais, horns and bowed cellos recall the opening before the final G-major chord.

composer.epithet: A conductor who composed in the summers, and wanted each symphony to hold a whole world — the sublime and the street band together.
facts: Vienna Conservatory, 1875–78: piano with Julius Epstein, composition with Franz Krenn; attended Bruckner’s university lectures
Budapest Royal Opera 1888–91 · Hamburg Stadttheater 1891–97 · Vienna Court Opera 1897–1907 · Metropolitan Opera and New York Philharmonic 1908–11
In summer huts at Steinbach am Attersee, Maiernigg on the Wörthersee, and Toblach in the Dolomites
Nine numbered symphonies and an unfinished Tenth; Das Lied von der Erde; orchestral songs

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. Iglau gave him the sounds that never left his music: bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church. A story he told late in life, to Sigmund Freud, describes running from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was grinding out Ach, du lieber Augustin. Tragedy and the banal, side by side: it is a fair description of half his slow movements.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, studying piano and composition, and sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. His friends were Hugo Wolf and the short-lived Hans Rott, whose symphony sounds so much like Mahler’s own that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony, as he understood it. The cantata Das klagende Lied, completed in 1880, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881. He had already begun the career that would pay for everything else: conducting.
